chapters.title: Chapter 1: Foundations of Market Making and Liquidity

lessons.title: SEBI's Designated Market Maker Scheme: How India Keeps Illiquid Options Tradeable

body.text: SEBI does not create liquidity in an illiquid contract by decree. It pays specific firms, through fee waivers and incentives, to be present with a firm two-way quote when almost nobody else will be, and calls that arrangement a Liquidity Enhancement Scheme.

children.text: The Problem This Scheme Actually Solves

Chapter 1's first lesson pointed at the gap: most individual stock options on NSE, and far-dated or deep out-of-the-money contracts across the board, are thin enough that an investor can find no one on the other side at any reasonable price. Left alone, this becomes self-reinforcing. Nobody wants to trade a contract they cannot exit easily, so volume stays low, so spreads stay wide, so even fewer people want to trade it. SEBI's answer to this trap is not a mandate that liquidity simply appear. It is a framework that lets exchanges pay specific firms to manufacture that liquidity on purpose.
How the Liquidity Enhancement Scheme Works

markDefs.definition: A SEBI-enabled framework under which a stock exchange identifies specific illiquid contracts and appoints one or more firms as market makers for them, in exchange for defined incentives, in return for defined two-way quoting obligations.

children.text: Since 2014, SEBI has permitted NSE and BSE to run a

for contracts they identify as illiquid, mainly in the equity derivatives segment. Within SEBI's broad framework, each exchange designs its own scheme: it names the specific contracts covered, appoints one or more market makers for them, and sets out exactly what those market makers must do in return for the benefits they receive. The obligations are built around continuous, firm, two-way quoting rather than one good quote and then silence, and the incentives are built around making that quoting commercially worthwhile even in a contract too thin to justify it on trading profit alone.

body.text: This lesson's title uses "Designated Market Maker" because that is the descriptive term many traders and financial media use in India for this role. In SEBI and exchange circulars themselves, the appointed firm is simply referred to as a "Market Maker" under the Liquidity Enhancement Scheme; "Designated Market Maker" as a formal title is more closely associated with specialist roles on exchanges like the NYSE. The underlying function described in this lesson is accurate to the Indian framework either way.

body.caption: The general shape of an LES arrangement (illustrative structure, not a specific current circular's exact thresholds)
headers: What the Exchange Offers in Return

cells: Maintain a live, firm quote for a large majority of the trading session, not just occasionally
Waiver or discount on exchange transaction charges
Keep the quoted bid-ask spread within a ceiling set by the exchange
Turnover-based cash incentive, subject to a defined cap
Quote at least a specified minimum order size on both the bid and the ask
Eligibility for additional trading or clearing benefits

body.text: The exact presence percentages, spread ceilings, and incentive amounts are set out per contract, per exchange, and are revised periodically. Do not treat the illustrative table above as current numbers to trade or model against; check the live NSE or BSE circular for the specific contract in question before relying on any figure.

body.title: How India's Market Maker Framework for Illiquid Derivatives Took Shape

events.title: SEBI Enables the Framework
events.description: SEBI issues a framework permitting stock exchanges to design their own Liquidity Enhancement Schemes for contracts identified as illiquid in the equity derivatives segment.

events.title: Exchanges Launch Contract-Specific Schemes
events.description: NSE and BSE begin running LES for selected illiquid stock options and futures, each with its own list of eligible contracts, market makers, and incentive structure.

events.title: Periodic Review
events.description: Exchanges periodically revise which contracts qualify as illiquid, and adjust market maker obligations and incentives, as trading volumes and market structure evolve.

body.text: The exchange is not being generous. A contract nobody can trade in and out of easily is a contract fewer people will use to begin with, whether to speculate, hedge, or discover a price for the underlying stock. Subsidising a market maker into an illiquid contract is a bet that manufactured liquidity attracts real liquidity, which in turn justifies the subsidy through higher overall volume.

children.text: Not the Same Thing as SME IPO Market Making

There is a second, unrelated use of the term market maker in Indian markets that is worth separating out clearly. Under SEBI's ICDR Regulations, a company listing on the SME platform of NSE or BSE is typically required to appoint a market maker, arranged through its merchant banker, to provide two-way quotes for a minimum period after listing. The purpose there is completely different: it exists because a newly listed small-cap stock, not a derivatives contract, can be so thinly traded in its first months that ordinary investors would otherwise struggle to exit at all, so the scheme exists to support orderly price discovery and an exit route right after listing, not to build a permanent liquidity venue for a derivatives contract.

body.title: LES Derivatives Market Making vs SME IPO Market Making

columns.label: LES (Equity Derivatives)
points: Applies to identified illiquid stock options and futures contracts
Market maker appointed and incentivised directly by the exchange
Runs on an ongoing basis for as long as the contract stays on the scheme
Goal: keep a derivatives contract tradeable so it stays useful for hedging and speculation

columns.label: SME Platform IPO Market Making
points: Applies to a newly listed SME-platform stock itself, not a derivative
Market maker arranged by the company's merchant banker under SEBI ICDR rules
Runs for a defined minimum period after listing, not indefinitely
Goal: support orderly price discovery and exit routes right after a small-cap listing

body.title: Which Scheme Applies?
body.question: A recently listed small-cap company on NSE's SME platform has a market maker quoting its shares for its first three months of trading. Which framework governs this arrangement?
options: SEBI's Liquidity Enhancement Scheme (LES) for equity derivatives
SEBI's ICDR Regulations requirement for SME platform listings
body.explanation: This is SME IPO market making under SEBI's ICDR Regulations, arranged through the company's merchant banker for a defined minimum period after listing. The Liquidity Enhancement Scheme is a different framework that applies to illiquid derivatives contracts, appointed and incentivised directly by the exchange rather than tied to a specific listing event.

body.text: An exchange incentive does not remove the underlying economics from the first three lessons of this chapter. A firm operating under LES still faces inventory risk if order flow runs one-sided, and still faces adverse selection if some of that flow is informed, exactly as any market maker does. The incentive only makes it commercially viable to accept those risks in a contract too thin to otherwise be worth the trouble.
